title: SATAN FOUGHT FOR MOSES’ DEAD BODY… BUT WHAT DID HE WANT WITH A CORPSE GOD HIMSELF HAD BURIED?
paragraphs: SATAN FOUGHT FOR MOSES’ DEAD BODY… BUT WHAT DID HE WANT WITH A CORPSE GOD HIMSELF HAD BURIED?

The Bible reveals a terrifying dispute over the remains of one of God's greatest servants. But the deeper you look, the more you discover a truth about death, accusation, spiritual warfare, and the authority of Jesus Christ that may change how you understand your own battles forever.
There is a strange moment in Scripture that almost nobody talks about.
A man is dead.
His mission is finished. His final breath has been taken. His body lies somewhere in the mountains of Moab, in a grave no human being can identify.
But something happens after his death.
Something so extraordinary that the New Testament mentions it centuries later.
Satan disputes over the dead body of Moses.
Not his staff.
Not the stone tablets.
Not the treasures of Egypt.
His corpse.
And the one confronting the devil is none other than Michael the archangel.
Now think about that for a moment.
Why would Satan concern himself with the remains of a man who was already dead?
What could the enemy possibly gain from a body whose soul he could not simply claim as his own?
And why does Scripture tell us that Michael did not pronounce his own condemnation against the devil, but instead declared:
“The Lord rebuke thee.” — Jude 1:9, KJV
There is something here that demands our attention.
But before we go any further, we must make a promise to the Word of God.
We will not invent a story where Scripture remains silent. We will not dress speculation in the clothing of revelation. And we will not turn an unexplained biblical event into a sensational doctrine.
Because the truth God has actually revealed is already powerful enough.
And when we follow that truth carefully, this mysterious conflict over a dead man's body leads us somewhere far greater than the grave of Moses.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
And perhaps, along the way, it will expose a battle taking place in your own heart.
Moses was not an ordinary man.

He was born under the shadow of a death sentence. Pharaoh had ordered Hebrew baby boys to be killed, yet God preserved this child through the courage of his mother and the unexpected compassion of Pharaoh's daughter.
The boy who should have died in the Nile grew up inside the palace of Egypt.
He experienced privilege while his people suffered in bondage.
Then everything changed.
Moses killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew and fled into the wilderness.
The man raised in royalty became a fugitive.
The palace gave way to the desert.
The future that once seemed secure collapsed into uncertainty.
And for forty years, Moses lived far away from the place where his story had begun.
Imagine the silence.
Imagine the memories.
Imagine a man who had once walked through the halls of power now walking behind sheep, wondering whether his greatest opportunity had already been wasted.
But God was not finished.
One day, a bush burned without being consumed.
And from the fire came a voice.
“Moses, Moses.” — Exodus 3:4
God called a man whose life had already been marked by fear, failure, exile, and regret.
That alone should speak to somebody reading this.
Your worst chapter does not necessarily get the final word.
Your past may explain where you have been, but it does not have the authority to cancel what God can accomplish through a surrendered life.
Moses returned to Egypt.
He confronted Pharaoh.
He witnessed the judgments of God.
He led Israel through the sea on dry ground.
He stood on Sinai while the mountain trembled.
He received the commandments of God.
He interceded for a rebellious nation.
And again and again, when Israel failed, Moses stood before the Lord and pleaded for mercy.
Yet Moses himself was not without sin.
That matters.
Because Scripture never presents him as a flawless superhero.
He was a servant of God who needed the grace of God.
And near the end of his life, one painful act of disobedience carried a consequence he could not reverse.
In Numbers 20, the Israelites were complaining about water. God instructed Moses to speak to the rock. Instead, Moses spoke rashly to the people and struck the rock twice.
Water still came out.
The people still drank.
But Moses had failed to honor God as holy before the congregation.
The Lord told him that he would not lead Israel into the Promised Land.
Imagine serving for decades, enduring rebellion, interceding through crisis after crisis, and then standing so close to the destination you had longed to reach.
Close enough to see it.
But not permitted to enter.
That is where the final earthly chapter of Moses unfolds.
Deuteronomy 34 tells us that Moses climbed Mount Nebo, where the Lord showed him the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Then Moses died.
He was one hundred and twenty years old.
Scripture says his eyesight had not grown dim and his natural vigor had not departed.
His death was not described as the collapse of a man whose strength had simply run out.
His appointed earthly journey had reached its end.
And then comes one of the most remarkable statements in the Old Testament.
“And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Beth-peor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.” — Deuteronomy 34:6, KJV
The Hebrew text reads:
וַיִּקְבֹּר אֹתוֹ בַגַּיְ בְּאֶרֶץ מוֹאָב
Vayyiqbor oto baggay be'eretz Mo'av.
“And he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab.”
The Hebrew verb vayyiqbor means “and he buried.” The subject is not explicitly named in that clause, but the natural reading in context identifies the Lord as the one who buried Moses.
Think about the tenderness of that scene.
The man who had spoken with God in extraordinary intimacy was laid to rest in a place known to God but hidden from humanity.
There was no famous tomb for pilgrims to visit.
No monument marking the location of his bones.
No shrine where future generations could gather around his remains.
The grave was unknown.
And then, hundreds of years later, Jude reveals something Deuteronomy does not describe.
“Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee.” — Jude 1:9, KJV
Read that again.
Michael.
The devil.
The body of Moses.
A dispute.
And a rebuke entrusted to the Lord.
In the original Greek, Jude writes:
περὶ τοῦ Μωϋσέως σώματος
Peri tou Mōyseōs sōmatos.
“Concerning the body of Moses.”
The Greek word sōma means “body.”
Jude is not merely saying that Satan attacked Moses' reputation or argued over his spiritual legacy.
The text explicitly concerns Moses' body.
The verse also uses the word διακρινόμενος (diakrinomenos), describing Michael as disputing or contending with the devil.
This was a real conflict as Jude presents it.
But here is the question that has occupied Bible readers for centuries.
Why?
Why would the devil dispute over the body of Moses?
The most important thing to understand is that Jude tells us the dispute happened, but does not tell us Satan's precise motive.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.

Some ancient Jewish traditions, known through later Christian references, associate this event with a work commonly called the Assumption of Moses or Testament of Moses. The surviving manuscript does not contain the dispute itself, so we cannot reconstruct the full story with certainty.
Some interpreters have proposed that Satan wanted to accuse Moses because of his sins, including the killing of the Egyptian.
Others have suggested that the devil wanted Moses' body to become an object of idolatrous worship.
Still others have connected the event with questions of burial, resurrection, or the spiritual significance of Moses' future appearance at the Transfiguration.
These are interpretations and possibilities.
They are not explanations explicitly given by Jude.
And we must be careful not to claim that the Bible has answered a question it leaves unanswered.
But that does not mean Jude 1:9 has nothing to teach us.
In fact, its central lesson may be even more searching than the mystery itself.
Look closely at what Michael did not do.
He did not rely upon an arrogant declaration of his own superiority.
He did not unleash a stream of insults against the devil.
He did not treat spiritual authority as permission for reckless speech.
Instead, he said:
“The Lord rebuke thee.”
The Greek is equally striking:
ἐπιτιμήσαι σοι κύριος
Epitimēsai soi Kyrios.
“May the Lord rebuke you.”
The verb expresses a rebuke or authoritative censure, and the wording places the authority in the Lord.
Jude uses this example while warning against arrogant people who speak abusively about things they do not understand.
That is the immediate context.
Michael's restraint stands in contrast to human presumption.
And there is a lesson here for every believer who has confused spiritual boldness with spiritual arrogance.
You do not become powerful by shouting louder than the enemy.
You do not become holy by pretending you possess authority independent of God.
You do not win spiritual battles by making yourself the center of them.
The authority belongs to the Lord.
That is not weakness.
That is dependence upon the One who has all authority.
And perhaps somebody needs to hear this because you have been fighting battles with nothing but your own strength.
You have been trying to overcome temptation through willpower alone.
Trying to heal wounds by pretending they do not hurt.
Trying to silence guilt by keeping yourself busy.
Trying to defeat darkness while neglecting prayer, repentance, and the Word of God.
And now you are exhausted.
You love Jesus, but you are tired.
You believe His promises, but your mind still returns to things you wish you had never done.
You know that forgiveness is possible, but some nights your memories sound louder than your faith.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to become impressed with your own spiritual strength.
The answer is to return to the Lord whose grace is sufficient.
James 4:7 says:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
Notice the order.
Submission to God comes before resistance to the devil.
Spiritual warfare is not a performance of human greatness.
It is a life of dependence upon God.
And this is where the story of Moses begins to reach into our own lives.
Moses was a great servant.
But Moses had sinned.
He had known fear.
He had known anger.
He had experienced the consequences of disobedience.
He had needed divine mercy.
And yet Scripture tells us that God Himself buried him.
His failure did not erase the reality of his relationship with the Lord.
His exclusion from Canaan did not mean that God had abandoned him.
And his death did not mean that God's redemptive purposes had come to an end.
Now consider something remarkable.
Centuries later, Jesus climbed a mountain with Peter, James, and John.
There, His appearance was transformed before them.
His face shone.
His garments became radiant.
And suddenly, two figures appeared with Him.
Moses.
And Elijah.
Matthew 17:3 says:
“And, behold, there appeared unto them Moses and Elias talking with him.”
The same Moses who had died outside the Promised Land was now appearing in glory with Jesus Christ.
Luke 9:31 tells us what they were discussing.
They spoke of Jesus' coming departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.
The Greek word used there is extraordinary:
ἔξοδος
Exodos.
“Departure” or “going out.”
It is the same Greek word from which we get the English word exodus.
Moses had once led Israel in the great exodus from Egypt.
Now he stood beside the Savior who was about to accomplish a far greater deliverance through His death and resurrection.
The first exodus brought a nation out of physical slavery.
The saving work of Jesus Christ delivers His people from the guilt and dominion of sin and ultimately from death itself.
Can you see the beauty of the connection?
Moses had led people through the sea.
Jesus would make a way through judgment and death.
Moses had mediated the old covenant.
Jesus would establish the new covenant through His blood.
Moses had pointed Israel toward a promised inheritance.
Jesus would secure an eternal inheritance for His redeemed people.
And Moses, who once stood on a mountain looking toward a land he could not enter during his earthly life, now stood with Christ in the land itself.
We should not pretend that the Transfiguration explains exactly why Satan disputed over Moses' body.
Scripture never makes that direct connection.
But the Transfiguration does show something beyond dispute.
The final significance of Moses' life was not determined by his grave. It was bound up with the glory of Jesus Christ.
And that is where this story becomes deeply personal.
Because the enemy does not need to possess your physical remains to exploit your fear, shame, or confusion.
Scripture identifies the devil as an accuser.
Revelation 12:10 calls him:
“the accuser of our brethren.”
The Greek word is κατήγωρ (katēgōr), meaning an accuser.
But we must understand this carefully.
The Bible does not say in Jude 1:9 that Satan was specifically accusing Moses of his past sins. That is one possible interpretation, not an established fact.
What Scripture clearly teaches elsewhere is that accusation is characteristic of Satan's opposition to God's people.
And many believers know the crushing experience of accusation.

Not every painful memory is a direct attack from the devil. Sometimes our conscience is rightly confronting us with sin that needs repentance. Sometimes trauma, grief, or anxiety requires patient care and wise support.
But there is a vital difference between conviction that leads us toward Christ and condemnation that tells us there is no hope in Christ.
The Holy Spirit convicts us of sin and leads us toward truth, repentance, and the Savior.
Condemnation without hope drives us toward despair.
One says, “Bring your sin into the light and turn to Jesus.”
The other whispers, “There is no point. You will never change.”
One reveals the wound so it can be treated.
The other insists that the wound is your entire identity.
Maybe you understand that distinction more personally than you want to admit.
You remember the relationship you destroyed.
The promise you broke.
The secret habit you keep returning to.
The moment anger made you say something you cannot take back.
The years you wasted running from God.
The people who trusted you and were disappointed.
And sometimes you wonder whether the Lord is as tired of your failures as you are.
You read about Moses and think about the Egyptian he killed.
You remember the rock he struck.
You remember that he never entered Canaan during his lifetime.
And you begin to wonder whether one terrible chapter can define an entire life.
But then you see Moses standing beside Jesus.
And you remember that grace is not the same as pretending sin never happened.
Grace does not rewrite history by calling evil good.
Grace changes the future of those who turn to God, because Jesus Christ has dealt with sin at the cross.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα
Ouden ara nyn katakrima.
“Therefore, now, no condemnation.”
The word katakrima refers to a condemnatory judgment.
Paul is not teaching that Christians never sin or never face loving correction.
He is proclaiming the astonishing reality that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemning verdict that their sins deserve.
Why?
Not because they have become flawless.
Not because their good deeds outweigh their evil deeds.
Not because they donated enough money, served enough ministries, or convinced enough people that they were religious.
But because Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
Romans 8:33–34 asks:
“Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again.”
There is the answer to every accusation against a person justified by faith in Jesus Christ.
Not denial.
Not self-righteousness.
Not excuses.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ interceding.
You may have a past that makes you ashamed.
But if you belong to Jesus, your past is not more powerful than His finished work.
You may have consequences that still hurt.
But consequences do not mean that forgiveness is impossible.
You may have tears you have never explained to anyone.
But the Lord sees what other people cannot.
And He calls sinners to come to Him.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Moses was forgiven and honored as God's servant, yet the consequences of his disobedience at Meribah remained.
David was forgiven, yet his household suffered painful consequences.
The thief on the cross received the promise of paradise, yet he still died upon his cross.
Grace is not an escape from every consequence.
Grace is the undeserved mercy of God that reconciles sinners to Himself through Jesus Christ.
And that is infinitely greater than merely having an easier life.
Now return to the mystery of Moses' burial.
God did not reveal the location of his grave.
Why?
Scripture does not explicitly tell us.
Some have suggested that concealing the grave prevented Israel from turning it into an object of worship.
That possibility fits the Bible's repeated warnings against idolatry, but it remains an inference rather than a stated reason.
Yet there is an unmistakable biblical principle here.
Even the greatest servant of God must never take the place of God.
Moses was faithful in God's house as a servant.
But Jesus is greater.
Hebrews 3:3 declares that Christ is worthy of more glory than Moses.
And in the Transfiguration, when Peter wanted to make three tabernacles—one for Jesus, one for Moses, and one for Elijah—a voice came from the cloud:
“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him.” — Matthew 17:5
Not “Worship Moses.”
Not “Build your life around Elijah.”
“Hear ye him.”
Jesus.
The beloved Son.
The fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets.
The One to whom Moses' ministry ultimately pointed.
That is the center of the entire Christian faith.
Not fascination with Satan.
Not endless speculation about a hidden grave.
Not obsession with spiritual mysteries that Scripture has not explained.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God who became flesh.
The sinless Savior who carried our sins.
The crucified Redeemer who rose from the dead.
The living Lord who will return in glory.
And that brings us to something even more astonishing.
The body of Moses was buried in a hidden place.
But the body of Jesus was placed in a known tomb.
Joseph of Arimathea took His body, wrapped it in clean linen, and laid it in a new tomb.
A stone was rolled across the entrance.
His followers grieved.
His enemies believed the threat had been contained.
For a moment, it appeared that death had silenced the One who called Himself the resurrection and the life.
But on the third day, the tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
Not merely as a beautiful memory.
Not as a symbol of hope.
Not as a spiritual idea.
The risen Jesus appeared to His disciples.
He showed them His wounds.
He ate in their presence.
He was alive.
And because He lives, death does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
Hebrews 2:14 says that through death, Christ acted to destroy the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil.
The Greek verb καταργήσῃ (katargēsē) carries the sense of rendering powerless, nullifying, or bringing to nothing in relation to the purpose described.
It does not mean that Satan has already ceased all activity.
The New Testament still warns believers to remain watchful against his schemes.
But it does mean that the decisive victory belongs to Christ.
The devil is not an equal rival to God.
He is a creature, not the Creator.
His power is limited.
His judgment is certain.
And Jesus Christ is Lord.
This is why Christians do not have to build their lives around fear of Satan.
We are called to stand firm in the Lord, put on the armor of God, resist the devil, remain sober-minded, pray, and hold fast to the truth.
And above all, we are called to look to Jesus.
The battle over Moses' body is mysterious.
The victory of Jesus Christ is not.
We do not know everything Satan intended in Jude 1:9.
But we know what Jesus accomplished at Calvary.
We know that His blood was shed for the forgiveness of sins.
We know that He rose from the dead.
We know that salvation is by grace through faith, not by human achievement.
And we know that everyone who truly comes to Christ in repentance and faith finds a Savior who is mighty to save.
Perhaps this is the moment where the article stops being about Moses.
And starts being about you.
Because maybe you have been carrying something dead for years.
An old identity.
An old failure.
An old wound.
An old bitterness.
An old secret.
Something you have buried beneath church attendance, religious language, and carefully managed appearances.
People see you smiling.
But they do not see the war inside.
They hear you say, “God is good.”
But they do not know how difficult it was for you to get out of bed that morning.
They see your Bible.
But they do not see the tears that fall onto its pages.
And maybe you are afraid that if people knew the full story, they would never look at you the same way again.
Listen.
You do not have to publish your deepest sins to prove that your repentance is sincere.
You do not have to expose your private wounds to strangers to demonstrate that God is healing you.
But you do need to stop believing that hiding from God can save you.
He already knows.
And the Gospel is not an invitation to pretend you are innocent.
It is an invitation for guilty sinners to come to the Savior who died for them.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is no need to decorate your confession.
No need to minimize the damage.
No need to blame everyone else.
Come honestly.
Repent sincerely.
Trust Christ completely.
And where your sin has harmed another person, seek to make things right where it is possible, wise, and safe to do so.
Because true grace does not teach us to cherish the chains from which Christ came to deliver us.
It teaches us to walk in newness of life.
This is what makes the Gospel so scandalous to human pride.
God does not save us because our stories are clean.
He saves sinners through the cleansing blood of Jesus.
He does not ask us to earn forgiveness by performing enough religious activity.
He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
He does not promise that following Him will remove every earthly sorrow.
He promises something greater.
His presence.
His mercy.
His transforming grace.
And the hope of resurrection.
Moses died outside Canaan.
But Moses was not outside the reach of God.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
But Jesus restored him.
Paul persecuted the church.
But the risen Christ confronted him, showed him mercy, and made him a witness of the Gospel.
The thief on the cross had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
But he turned to Jesus and heard the promise of paradise.
Different stories.
Different failures.
Different consequences.
The same extraordinary Savior.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because justice was unnecessary.
But because Jesus bore the judgment that sinners could never remove by their own efforts.
And His resurrection declares that death itself will not have the last word.
Maybe you came here because you were curious about a strange verse in Jude.
You wanted to know why Satan disputed over Moses' corpse.
You expected an explanation of an ancient spiritual confrontation.
But perhaps God has used that question to bring you face-to-face with something far more important.
What will you do with Jesus Christ?
You can spend years investigating mysteries about the devil and still neglect the Savior.
You can memorize details about angels and never surrender your pride.
You can argue about Moses' burial and remain unwilling to bury the sins you keep defending.
You can know the vocabulary of spiritual warfare and still refuse the daily obedience of faith.
Do not let fascination with the unseen distract you from the One Scripture has clearly revealed.
Jesus is not asking you to solve every mystery before you come to Him.
He is calling you to trust Him.
And if your heart is convicted right now, do not harden it.
You can pray honestly:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to turn away from sin and follow You. I surrender my life to You. Make me new, not through my strength, but through Your grace. Amen.”
A prayer is not a magical formula.
The words themselves do not purchase salvation.
Salvation belongs to the Lord, and the call of the Gospel is genuine repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
But if those words express the sincere cry of your heart, do not treat that cry as insignificant.
Bring it to Him.
And then keep following Him.
Open His Word.
Pray.
Seek fellowship with a faithful, Bible-teaching church.
Learn to obey Him in ordinary life.
Confess when you sin.
Receive correction.
Extend forgiveness.
Love your neighbor.
And keep your eyes fixed upon Christ.
Because Christianity is not merely the excitement of one emotional moment.
It is a life of following the crucified and risen Lord.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn the mysteries of Scripture into entertainment.
Not to glorify darkness.
Not to make a personality, platform, or ministry more important than Jesus.
But to keep pointing people back to the Word of God and the Savior it reveals.
Somebody in your Facebook friends list may be fighting a battle you know nothing about.
A brother who has stopped praying.
A sister who feels ashamed to return to church.
A father who thinks he has ruined everything.
A young person who believes their past has destroyed their future.
Someone who has never understood why the death and resurrection of Jesus matter.
Not merely because it is interesting, but because someone may need to hear the Gospel through it.
Or perhaps:
“I'm still fighting, but I'm holding on to Jesus.”
You do not need to tell strangers every detail of your struggle. But your honest words may remind another believer that they are not alone in their need for grace.
There is no shame in asking your brothers and sisters in Christ to pray.
We want people to encounter the truth of God's Word, not merely another stream of religious content.
Those free resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment available to people who may not be able to afford it.
But there is also an opportunity for those who are able and willing to help sustain and expand this work.
And we want to be clear about something important.
The Bible teaches believers to give willingly, generously, and without compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, thoughtful gifts, or practical resources for daily encouragement.
It is helping Gospel-centered teaching and discipleship resources reach people who need them.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage someone.
Invite others to study the Word.
Your prayers, your testimony, and your willingness to share biblical truth matter.
The work of God has never depended upon the purchasing power of His people.
It depends upon the Lord who gives the increase.
And now, before you leave, return with me one last time to that lonely mountain in Moab.
An old servant of God has died.
His body is buried.
His grave is hidden.
Jude tells us that Michael disputed with the devil concerning that body.
We are not told exactly what Satan wanted.
We are not told every word spoken in that encounter.
We are not given permission to fill the silence with invented revelations.
But we are shown a heavenly messenger who appeals to the authority of the Lord.
And we are shown, elsewhere in Scripture, the same Moses appearing in glory beside Jesus Christ.
The mystery remains.
But the message is clear.
No created being is greater than the Lord.
No servant, however faithful, is greater than Jesus.
No human failure is beyond the forgiveness Christ offers to repentant sinners.
And no grave can defeat the resurrection power of God.
One day, those who belong to Christ will rise.
Not because they lived without mistakes.
Not because they conquered death through personal determination.
Not because they knew every secret of the spiritual world.
But because Jesus Christ died and rose again.
First Corinthians 15:57 declares:
“But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.”
So when your past accuses you, do not pretend it never happened.
Bring it to the cross.
When temptation comes, do not trust your own strength.
Submit to God and stand firm in His truth.
When death frightens you, remember the empty tomb.
And when your life feels like a story that has gone terribly wrong, remember that the Lord who restored Peter, showed mercy to Paul, and received the dying thief is still calling sinners to Himself.
Your story may contain scandal.
It may contain shame.
It may contain consequences that cannot be undone.
But in Jesus Christ, repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and a transformed life can begin.
The devil disputed over the body of Moses, but the greater truth is that Jesus Christ has conquered the grave itself.
And perhaps the most important question was never what Satan wanted from a dead man.
Perhaps it is whether you will trust the living Savior who gave His life to redeem sinners.
The grave may hold the evidence of where your earthly story ended, but it can never erase the promise of resurrection spoken by the One who walked out of His own.
